title: Text & Data Wrangling
summary: Master grep, awk, sed, and jq — the tools you use every day without fully knowing.

sections.title: grep — find what you need
sections.body:
## grep: Finding Signals in the Noise

In DevOps, you are constantly looking for specific information inside large streams of text: error messages in application logs, failing pods in `kubectl` output, misconfigured values in Helm manifests, or suspicious patterns in audit logs. `grep` is the foundational tool for this task — it scans input line by line and prints only the lines that match a pattern.

While grep's basic usage is simple, its real power comes from a handful of flags that dramatically expand what you can do with it. The `-E` flag enables extended regular expressions, letting you match complex patterns without escaping every special character. The `-v` flag inverts the match, which is essential for filtering out noise (like removing `Running` pods from a pod list to show only the problematic ones). The `-A`, `-B`, and `-C` flags add surrounding context to matches, which is invaluable when debugging — a single error line rarely tells the full story without the lines before and after it.

In a Kubernetes environment specifically, grep is your first line of investigation: scanning events for `BackOff` or `OOMKilled`, finding all pods not in a healthy state, or auditing manifests for image tags before a deployment. The pattern of piping `kubectl` output through grep — often multiple times — is one of the most common idioms you will encounter in real cluster operations.

The key mental model for grep is: **it selects lines**. Everything else — context, inversion, regex — is just about making the selection more precise.

```bash
# Basic grep
grep 'Error' app.log

# -E: extended regex (use this by default)
grep -E 'Error|WARN' app.log

# -i: case insensitive
grep -i 'oomkilled' kubectl-events.log

# -v: invert (lines that DON'T match)
grep -v '^#' config.yaml     # remove comment lines

# -A/-B/-C: lines After/Before/Context
grep -A 5 'BackOff' pod.log   # 5 lines after each match

# -o: print only the matching part
grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' access.log  # extract IPs

# Useful in DevOps:
# Find all image tags in k8s manifests
grep -rE 'image:\s+\S+' ./helm-charts/

# Find pods NOT in Running state from kubectl output
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed | grep -v NAME
```

sections.title: awk — process columns and patterns
sections.body:
## awk: Structured Text Processing

Where grep selects lines, `awk` lets you work with the **structure within those lines**. `awk` treats each line as a record and automatically splits it into fields separated by whitespace (or any delimiter you specify with `-F`). This makes it the natural tool for processing the column-based output that most Unix tools produce — including `kubectl`, `docker ps`, `ps aux`, and `/etc/passwd`.

`awk` is effectively a small programming language embedded in a single command. It runs a program against each input line: you can test conditions (`$4 != "Running"`), perform arithmetic (summing a cost column), format output with `printf`, and accumulate results across lines with the `END` block. For most DevOps tasks, you only need a small subset of this: field access (`$1`, `$2`, `NR`), simple conditions, and the `print` statement.

The two most common `awk` patterns in Kubernetes work are: **column extraction** (pull the name or status field from `kubectl get pods` output) and **conditional filtering** (print only lines where the status field is not `Running`). Both of these are cleaner in `awk` than in a combination of `cut`, `grep`, and `tr` because `awk` handles variable-width whitespace naturally — the `kubectl` table format pads columns with spaces, which trips up `cut` but is invisible to `awk`.

`awk` also excels at cross-namespace audits: a single `kubectl get pods -A | awk '...'` pipeline can scan every namespace simultaneously and apply per-row logic that would require a loop in any other approach.

awk processes text line by line. Fields are split by whitespace (or a delimiter you set).

```bash
# $1, $2... are fields. $0 is the whole line. NR is line number.
kubectl get pods | awk '{print $1, $3}'  # NAME and STATUS columns

# Skip header line
kubectl get pods | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}'

# Filter by pattern in a field
kubectl get pods -A | awk '$4 != "Running" && $4 != "STATUS" {print $1, $2, $4}'

# Sum a column (great for AWS costs)
aws ce get-cost-and-usage ... | awk -F'"' '/Amount/ {sum += $4} END {print "Total: $" sum}'

# Custom delimiter with -F
cat /etc/passwd | awk -F: '{print $1, $6}'  # username and home dir

# Multiple conditions
kubectl get pods -A | awk '
    $4 == "CrashLoopBackOff" { print "CRASH:", $1, $2 }
    $4 == "OOMKilled"        { print "OOM:",   $1, $2 }
'

# Practical: get all non-running pods across namespaces
kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | \
    awk '$4 !~ /Running|Completed|Succeeded/ {printf "%-30s %-40s %s\n", $1, $2, $4}'
```

sections.title: sed — stream editor for substitutions
sections.body:
## sed: Surgical Substitution on Text Streams

`sed` (stream editor) occupies a specific and important niche: it is the right tool when you know the pattern you want to change and you want to change it, either in a stream or directly in a file. While `grep` finds and `awk` processes, `sed` **transforms** — replacing one string or pattern with another, deleting lines that match a pattern, or extracting specific line ranges from a file.

In DevOps work, `sed` appears most frequently in two contexts. The first is **templating**: updating a Helm values file, a Kubernetes manifest, or a `.env` file with environment-specific values before applying it. The `sed -i` flag (in-place editing) makes this safe and scriptable — you modify the file directly without needing to redirect to a temporary file and move it back. The second context is **log processing**: stripping comment lines from a config before parsing it, removing blank lines before counting, or extracting specific line ranges from a large log file.

The core `sed` command is the substitution: `s/pattern/replacement/flags`. The `g` flag replaces all occurrences on a line (not just the first). The `-E` flag enables extended regex (same as `grep -E`). The `|` delimiter can replace `/` when your pattern or replacement contains forward slashes — common when working with file paths or URLs.

Knowing when to reach for `sed` versus `awk` is a judgment call that comes with practice. The rough guide: if you are doing **substitution** or **line deletion**, use `sed`. If you are doing **field extraction**, **conditional logic**, or **arithmetic**, use `awk`.

sed is best at find-and-replace on streams.

```bash
# Basic substitution: s/pattern/replacement/flags
echo 'image: nginx:latest' | sed 's/latest/1.25.3/'

# g flag: replace ALL occurrences on each line
echo 'foo foo foo' | sed 's/foo/bar/g'

# -i: edit file in place (use -i.bak for a backup)
sed -i.bak 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' deployment.yaml

# Delete lines matching pattern
sed '/^#/d' config.yaml       # delete comment lines
sed '/^$/d' config.yaml       # delete empty lines

# Print only matching lines (like grep)
sed -n '/Error/p' app.log

# Extract a range of lines
sed -n '10,20p' large-file.log

# Practical: update image tag in a values file
NEW_TAG="v1.2.3"
sed -i "s|tag: .*|tag: ${NEW_TAG}|" values.yaml

# Replace a specific key=value in a .env file
sed -i "s|^AWS_REGION=.*|AWS_REGION=eu-west-1|" .env
```

When to use sed vs awk:
- **sed**: substitution, deletion, line ranges — when you know the pattern and want to change it
- **awk**: column processing, conditions, arithmetic — when you need to reason about fields

sections.title: jq — JSON is your daily driver now
sections.body:
## jq: The Essential Tool for a JSON-First World

Modern infrastructure tools speak JSON. `kubectl` outputs JSON. The AWS CLI outputs JSON. GitLab, Harbor, ArgoCD, Vault, Terraform — all of their APIs and CLI tools return JSON. If you are doing DevOps work in 2024 and beyond, you are processing JSON constantly, and doing it well requires `jq`.

`jq` is a command-line JSON processor with its own small query language. At its simplest, it pretty-prints JSON and extracts single fields. At its most powerful, it filters arrays by conditions, reshapes objects, performs string interpolation, and formats output as tab-separated values that can feed into the rest of your pipeline. The key insight is that `jq` is not just for reading JSON — it is for **transforming** JSON into whatever shape your next tool needs.

The learning curve for `jq` is front-loaded. The first few concepts — `.` for the root object, `.field` for field access, `.[]` to iterate an array, `select()` to filter, `-r` for raw string output — cover roughly 90% of real-world usage. The remaining 10% covers more advanced operations like building new objects with `{key: .value}`, using `@tsv` and `@csv` output formats, and combining filters with `|` (the jq pipe, analogous to the shell pipe).

A professional habit worth developing: **always build jq queries incrementally**. Start with `.` to see the full structure, then drill down one level at a time (`keys`, `.[0]`, `.field`), then add `select()` filters. This exploratory approach is faster than trying to write the perfect query from memory, and it works on any new API response you encounter.

jq is essential for working with kubectl, AWS CLI, GitLab API, Harbor API, Terraform output.

```bash
# Pretty print
kubectl get pod my-pod -o json | jq .

# Extract a single field
kubectl get pod my-pod -o json | jq '.status.phase'

# Iterate over array
kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[] | .metadata.name'

# Multiple fields as object
kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, status: .status.phase}'

# Filter array by condition
kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.phase != "Running") | .metadata.name'

# -r: raw output (no quotes around strings)
kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name'

# Real patterns you'll use with AWS CLI:
# List all EC2 instances with their state
aws ec2 describe-instances | jq -r \
    '.Reservations[].Instances[] | [.InstanceId, .InstanceType, .State.Name] | @tsv'

# Get images from ECR repo
aws ecr list-images --repository-name my-repo | \
    jq -r '.imageIds[] | select(.imageTag != null) | .imageTag' | sort

# ArgoCD: get all apps not Synced
argocd app list -o json | \
    jq -r '.[] | select(.status.sync.status != "Synced") | .metadata.name'

# Harbor: get robot accounts
curl -s https://harbor.example.com/api/v2.0/robots \
    -H "Authorization: Basic $HARBOR_TOKEN" | \
    jq -r '.[] | [.name, .level, .disable] | @tsv'

# Build a jq query step by step:
# 1. See full structure first:
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq 'keys'
# 2. Drill down:
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[0] | keys'
# 3. Find what you need:
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[0].status.conditions'
# 4. Filter:
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].status.conditions[] | select(.type=="Ready") | {name: .status}'
```

sections.title: String manipulation without external tools
sections.body:
## String Manipulation Without External Tools

When you need to transform a string in bash — strip a file extension, extract a version number from an image tag, convert a cluster name to uppercase — the instinct is often to reach for `sed`, `cut`, or `awk`. These tools work, but each one spawns a new subprocess, which has a measurable cost when called repeatedly in a loop (for example, processing hundreds of pod names).

Bash has a built-in set of **parameter expansion** operators that handle the most common string operations without spawning any subprocess at all. These operators work on any variable and use a consistent pattern: `${variable<operator><pattern>}`. The `##` and `%%` operators strip prefixes and suffixes (longest match), the `%` and `#` operators strip shorter matches, the `/` operator replaces substrings, and the `^^`/`,,` operators change case.

Understanding these operators also improves your ability to read other people's bash scripts — they are ubiquitous in production DevOps tooling. A line like `${FILE##*/}` (get filename from path) or `${IMAGE%:*}` (strip tag from image reference) appears constantly in deployment scripts, and being able to parse it at a glance saves significant time when debugging.

The practical guideline: **use parameter expansion for simple transformations on individual strings**, and reach for `sed`/`awk` when you need to process multiple lines or apply more complex patterns. The boundary is blurry, but the performance and readability benefits of parameter expansion are worth knowing about.

Pure bash string operations — faster than spawning a subprocess.

```bash
FILE="/path/to/my-service-v1.2.3.yaml"

# Get filename from path (like basename)
echo "${FILE##*/}"          # my-service-v1.2.3.yaml

# Get directory (like dirname)
echo "${FILE%/*}"           # /path/to

# Strip extension
echo "${FILE%.*}"           # /path/to/my-service-v1.2.3

# Get extension
echo "${FILE##*.}"          # yaml

# Substring
STR="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
echo "${STR:0:8}"           # eks-prod (start:length)

# Replace
echo "${STR/prod/staging}"  # eks-staging-mach-x7kq
echo "${STR//k/K}"          # replace all occurrences

# Uppercase / lowercase
echo "${STR^^}"             # EKS-PROD-MACH-X7KQ
echo "${STR,,}"             # eks-prod-mach-x7kq

# Check if string contains substring
if [[ "$STR" == *"prod"* ]]; then
    echo "This is a production cluster!"
fi

# Check if starts/ends with
[[ "$STR" == eks-* ]] && echo "EKS cluster"
[[ "$FILE" == *.yaml ]] && echo "YAML file"

# String length
echo "${#STR}"              # 17
```

sections.title: Exercise: kubectl pod health reporter
sections.body:
## Combining the Tools: A Real Reporting Script

Real DevOps scripts rarely use a single text-processing tool in isolation. A typical workflow chains several tools together: `kubectl` produces JSON, `jq` extracts and filters the relevant fields into tab-separated output, a `while read` loop processes each row, and `awk` or bash string operations format the final report. This exercise gives you practice with exactly that pattern.

Pod health reporting is one of the most common operational tasks in Kubernetes environments. Operators need to quickly identify which pods are not running normally, understand why (crash loop, OOMKilled, pending), and prioritize their attention (high restart counts indicate instability that needs investigation). A well-structured report groups this information by namespace and highlights the most critical issues at a glance.

The key technique here is the `jq` to `while IFS=$'\t' read` pattern: `jq -r '... | @tsv'` formats structured data as tab-separated lines, and `while IFS=$'\t' read -r col1 col2 ...'` splits each line on tabs into named variables. This combination is more robust than parsing space-separated output because field values can contain spaces without breaking the parsing.

As you implement this script, pay attention to how you track state (the current namespace) across loop iterations, and how you use bash string comparison (`[[ $restarts -gt 5 ]]`) to add conditional highlighting. These are patterns you will use in almost every reporting script you write.

Write a script `pod-health.sh` that:

1. Runs `kubectl get pods -A -o json`
2. Uses `jq` to extract: namespace, name, phase, restartCount, and image
3. Prints a formatted report of pods that are NOT Running/Succeeded
4. Groups output by namespace
5. Highlights pods with restartCount > 5

Expected output format:
```
=== Namespace: kube-system ===
  [WARN] coredns-abc123 | CrashLoopBackOff | restarts: 8 | image: coredns/coredns:1.9.3

=== Namespace: argocd ===
  [OK]   argocd-server-xyz | Running | restarts: 0 | image: argoproj/argocd:v2.14.0
```

Skeleton:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Get pod data as TSV: namespace, name, phase, restarts, image
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '
    .items[] |
    [
        .metadata.namespace,
        .metadata.name,
        .status.phase // "Unknown",
        # TODO: get restart count from containerStatuses
        # TODO: get first container image
    ] | @tsv
' | sort | while IFS=$'\t' read -r ns name phase restarts image; do
    # TODO: format output, group by namespace, flag high restarts
    echo "$ns | $name | $phase | $restarts | $image"
done
```

Hints:
- jq: `.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount // 0`
- jq: `.spec.containers[0].image`
- Track current namespace with a variable to print headers
- Use `[[ $restarts -gt 5 ]]` for the restart check
